extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and advanced law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether an alleged invention satisfies statutory novelty, prior-use, public-use/on-sale, foreign-publication, and usefulness requirements (including treatment of "lost arts", process vs product distinctions, and licensee defenses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory novelty / first inventor requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter must be new and the patentee must be the "original and first inventor"; the invention must be "not known or used by others before his discovery or invention."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clause requires that the applicant verily believes himself to be first inventor and permits the negative to be shown in defense. The court treats prior existence or use by others as potentially negating the patentee's status as first inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of lost or forgotten arts (two classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish two classes of 'lost' or 'abandoned' arts: (1) where an existing article discloses its mode of manufacture (knowledge and means of knowledge are the same); (2) where the article exists but the process/mode of manufacture cannot be inferred from the article and is unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the first class, production of the article itself may prove prior knowledge/use regardless of whether witnesses had 'forgotten' it; in the second class, the newly discovered process may be a true invention because the old method is unknown and cannot be shown to be the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production of a prior machine/article as anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: The production of a previously existing machine or article of manufacture (with or without proof of actual user) may vitiate subsequent letters-patent for the same machine or article by showing it previously existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the produced article shows its mode of manufacture matters: if inspection reveals the mode, prior existence defeats the later patent; if not, mere production of the article may be insufficient to prove the prior process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and testing of witness recollection in prior-use proof
rubrics_metrics.description: When priority depends on witness recollection of prior existence or use, the accuracy of that recollection must be tested; forgetting and later recollection (possibly stimulated by later inventions) affects weight but not necessarily admissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A witness's having forgotten a former article may be relevant to the accuracy of his description and whether he unconsciously borrowed from a subsequent specimen; but if a witness can accurately describe the prior thing, it proves prior knowledge/use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-vs-product distinction for "use" and "knowledge"
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether prior 'use' or 'knowledge' defeats a patent depends on the character of the subject-matter: for machines the thing itself may suffice, but for arts/products where the invention is the process, prior production of the product alone does not necessarily show prior knowledge/use of the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The words 'the thing patented' and 'it' should be applied to the appropriate subject—e.g., in an art the 'thing' may be the process rather than the product; mere prior manufacture by an unknown art does not necessarily negative a subsequent inventor's claim to a novel process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical/foreign prior-use and publication rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior knowledge or use in a foreign country does not, by itself, void a U.S. patent if the subject had not been patented or described in printed publication abroad, provided the patentee believed himself to be first inventor at time of application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute's proviso protects an honest inventor from foreign prior use unless there was a prior foreign patent or printed publication describing the invention (or substantial part thereof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of a prior patent or printed publication to defeat a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior foreign patent or printed publication relied on to defeat a patent must 'contain and exhibit a substantial representation of the patented improvement in such full, clear, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art or science ... to make, construct, and practise the invention to the same practical extent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere vague or general representations will not support the defense; the prior disclosure must be an account of a complete and operative invention sufficiently enabling for a skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use or sale with inventor's consent as bar (abandonment/dedication)
rubrics_metrics.description: If, at the time of application, the invention was in public use or on sale with the inventor's consent or allowance, the inventor may have lost the right to a patent; public use or sale by consent prior to application can operate as abandonment or dedication to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recognizes a distinction between abandoning/dedicating before applying (which can bar a patent) and abandoning a patent right after it issues. Courts have treated voluntary public use or sale by the inventor as creating a disability to obtain a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-year prior-use safe harbor for individual permitted uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory amendment (act of 1839, §7) limited the forfeiture effect of individual prior uses with the inventor's consent to uses occurring more than two years before the application; such prior licensees/purchasers keep a right to use the specific machine/manufacture/composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventor may permit use by individuals for up to two years prior to application and still obtain a valid patent; use longer than two years or general abandonment to the public will invalidate the patent as to others (but prior licensees retain their rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who qualifies as a licensee by operation of law / scope of prior-user protection
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim benefit as a licensee by operation of law, the person must be a purchaser or have used the invention before the patent was issued by license/grant/consent of the inventor (not a mere wrong-doer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an employee who made experiments in the employer's manufactory, permitted employer's use without compensation being demanded, and then obtained a patent — such unmolested and notorious prior use may bring the case within the statute and protect the prior user.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory usefulness (utility) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be 'useful' in the statutory sense: capable of some beneficial use and not injurious to the welfare, morals, health, or order of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law does not inquire into degree of utility; it suffices that the invention is not noxious or mischievous and can be applied to practical uses. Comparative utility (better/worse than alternatives) is a separate test often used in novelty/substantial-difference inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: False suggestion or misleading specification as ground for invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: If part of a specification is useless or the patent contains a false suggestion calculated to mislead the public, that may render the patent void (i.e., the inquiry whether a claimed part is useless relates to false suggestion/misleading).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish statutory 'useful' requirement from questions about whether particular claimed elements are essential or are misleadingly presented in the specification.
